entry: American [[Punk rock]] band, formed in Forest Hills, [[Queens]], [[New York City]], in 1974. Often recognized as one of the first punk bands, the Ramones never achieved significant commercial success but were highly influential. Members adopted pseudonyms ending in Ramone, inspired by [[Paul McCartney]], who had used the stage name Paul Ramon. The band performed 2,263 concerts and released fourteen studio albums in 22 years of nonstop touring. It disbanded in 1996 after a farewell concert in [[Los Angeles]]. Inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2002, the band received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2011.

1985 epic historical action drama directed by [[Akira Kurosawa]]. The plot derives from *King Lear* by [[William Shakespeare]] and includes segments based on legends of the daimyō Mōri Motonari. It stars Tatsuya Nakadai as Hidetora Ichimonji, an aging warlord who divides his domain among three sons. With a budget of $11–12 million, it was among the most expensive films in Japanese cinema history at its release. Emi Wada won an Academy Award for Best Costume Design, and Kurosawa received his only career nomination for Best Director. The score, inspired by [[Gustav Mahler]], was composed by Toru Takemitsu.

Queen regnant of [[Madagascar]] (r. 1828–1861). Ranavalona I took the throne after the death of her husband, Radama I, and pursued isolationism and self-sufficiency. She reduced ties with European powers and suppressed the Malagasy Christian movement that had begun under Radama I with members of the London Missionary Society. She used forced labor, called *fanompoana*, for public works and to maintain a standing army of between 20,000 and 30,000 Merina soldiers. Warfare, [[Slavery|slavery]], disease, forced labor and the *tangena* poison ordeal caused high mortality, and by some estimates the population declined by as much as half during her 33-year reign. European contemporaries called her a tyrant and the "Mad Monarch of Madagascar", a view that persisted in Western scholarship until the mid-1970s. Later academic research saw her as protecting Malagasy sovereignty against European influence. She remains a controversial figure, largely viewed negatively in Madagascar today.

Indian actor who works in Hindi-language films. The son of actors Rishi Kapoor and Neetu Singh, and grandson of [[Raj Kapoor]], he made his acting debut in *Saawariya* (2007). He gained prominence with *Wake Up Sid* and *Ajab Prem Ki Ghazab Kahani* (both 2009). His performances in *Rockstar* (2011) and *Barfi!* (2012) won him two consecutive Filmfare Awards for Best Actor. He later won another Filmfare Award for playing Sanjay Dutt in *Sanju* (2018) and a fourth Best Actor award for *Animal* (2023). His highest-grossing release is *Ramayana: Part 1* (2026). He is married to actress [[Alia Bhatt]].

Capital and largest district by population of the Indian state of [[Jharkhand]] (pop., 2011: 1,073,427). Ranchi was the center of the Jharkhand movement, which called for a separate state for tribal regions of South Bihar, northern Odisha, western West Bengal and eastern Chhattisgarh. The state was formed on 15 November 2000 from Bihar divisions. Ranchi is being developed as a smart city under [[Narendra Modi]]'s flagship Smart Cities Mission. Located on the Ranchi Plateau, at an average elevation of 700 meters, the city is nicknamed the City of Waterfalls. Its historic sights include the Jagannath Temple and Ratu Palace. Universities and medical colleges are among its institutions, and its economy includes agriculture, mining and services.

Form of electronic computer memory that can be read and written in almost the same time regardless of the physical location of data. RAM typically stores working data and machine code. In modern technology it takes the form of [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuit]] chips with MOS memory cells. The two main volatile types are static RAM (SRAM) and dynamic RAM (DRAM), which lose stored information when power is removed. Semiconductor RAM dates to 1965, when [[IBM]] introduced the monolithic 16-bit SP95 SRAM chip for its System/360 Model 95 computer. In 1966 Robert Dennard invented the modern DRAM architecture, with a single MOS transistor per capacitor. The first commercial DRAM chip, the 1K [[Intel]] 1103, appeared in October 1970. Synchronous DRAM (SDRAM) was reintroduced with the [[Samsung]] KM48SL2000 chip in 1992.

Measurable function modeling a quantity or object that depends on random events. Its domain is the set of possible outcomes in a sample space, and its range is typically a subset of the [[Real number|real numbers]]. Despite the name, the mathematical definition refers neither to randomness nor to variability, but to a [[Function (mathematics)|function]]. Its distribution is the pushforward measure, a probability measure on its possible values. Two random variables may have identical distributions yet differ in significant ways, for instance by being independent. Discrete random variables take values in a countable set, while absolutely continuous ones take values in an interval and are described by a [[Probability density function|probability density function]]. Any random variable can be described by its [[Cumulative distribution function|cumulative distribution function]]. Key properties include the [[Expected value|expected value]] and [[Variance|variance]].

Form of [[Experiment|experiment]] that evaluates the efficacy or safety of an intervention by randomly allocating participants to comparison groups. One group receives the intervention under study, while others receive an alternative treatment, a [[Placebo|placebo]] or standard care. Randomized controlled trials are widely considered among the highest-quality sources of evidence in evidence-based medicine, because random allocation reduces selection bias and the influence of confounding factors, though they have been criticized for failing to reduce bias in some cases. A well-blinded trial is considered the gold standard for clinical trials. In *Ortus Medicinae* (1648), Jan Baptist van Helmont proposed a trial of two fever treatments, but probably never conducted it. The first reported clinical trial, by James Lind in 1747, tested treatments for [[Scurvy]]. The modern form emerged with a 1948 British Medical Research Council trial of streptomycin for pulmonary [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]], which used sealed envelopes for random allocation.

American professional wrestler, rapper and baseball player. Signed by the St. Louis Cardinals as a catcher, he later became known for his time in the World Wrestling Federation (WWF, later [[WWE]]) and World Championship Wrestling (WCW). He had ten world championship reigns during a 32-year career, including two as WWF World Heavyweight Champion and four as WCW World Heavyweight Champion. He headlined WrestleMania IV and WrestleMania V. His entrance music was the finale of Edward Elgar's *Pomp and Circumstance March no. 1*, and his catchphrase was "Oooh yeah!" He was inducted posthumously into the WWE Hall of Fame in 2015.

Indian actress who works in Hindi films. She has received a National Film Award and eight Filmfare Awards. She began acting as a teenager in her father Ram Mukherjee's Bengali film *Biyer Phool* (1996) and broke through with *Kuch Kuch Hota Hai* (1998). She was praised for playing an abused wife in *Yuva* (2004). After critics had faulted her choice of roles, she was praised as a headstrong journalist in *No One Killed Jessica* (2011). *Mrs. Chatterjee vs Norway* (2023) earned her the National Film Award for Best Actress. She is married to filmmaker [[Aditya Chopra]].

Family of [[Frog|frogs]], sometimes called true frogs, with the widest distribution of any frog family. They occur on all continents except Antarctica, including North America, Europe, Africa (including [[Madagascar]]) and Asia. Typically smooth and moist-skinned, with large, powerful legs and extensively webbed feet, true frogs range from small species such as the wood frog to large ones. Many are aquatic or live near water, and most lay their eggs in water and pass through a tadpole stage. The family includes arboreal species and some of the few amphibians able to live in [[Brackish water|brackish water]]. The family began dispersing from Asia at the end of the [[Eocene]], reaching every continent except Antarctica by the beginning of the Miocene. Earlier work placed its origin on India, but more recent studies propose Eurasia.

Indian actor who works in Hindi films and is among India's highest-paid actors. He won the Filmfare Award for Best Male Debut for *Band Baaja Baaraat* (2010). He then starred in period dramas directed by Sanjay Leela Bhansali, including *Bajirao Mastani* (2015), for which he won the Filmfare Award for Best Actor, and *Padmaavat* (2018), in which he played [[Alauddin Khalji|Sultan Alauddin Khalji]]. He later won Filmfare Best Actor awards for *Gully Boy* (2019) and *83* (2021). The spy thrillers *Dhurandhar* (2025) and *Dhurandhar: The Revenge* (2026) rank among the five highest-grossing Indian films. He is married to actress [[Deepika Padukone]].

Type of [[Sexual assault|sexual assault]] involving sexual intercourse or other penetration carried out without [[Consent|consent]]. It may be committed through physical force, coercion, or sex with someone unable to give valid consent, such as a person who is incapacitated, has an intellectual disability, or is below the age of consent ([[Statutory rape|statutory rape]]). Victims are often traumatized and may develop [[Post-traumatic stress disorder|post-traumatic stress disorder]]. Rape can also cause serious injury and carries the risk of [[Sexually transmitted infection|sexually transmitted infections]], and victims assigned female at birth face the risk of pregnancy. It is a serious crime in most jurisdictions, although most do not criminalize the rape of men. Widespread rape during conflict is a crime against humanity and a [[War crime|war crime]], and rape committed with intent to destroy an ethnic group can be an element of [[Genocide|genocide]]. Until 2012 the Federal Bureau of Investigation considered rape a crime committed solely by men against women.

Yellow-flowered member of the [[Brassicaceae]] family, grown primarily for its oil-rich seed. Also known as rape, oilseed rape and canola, it is the third-largest source of [[Vegetable oil|vegetable oil]] and the second-largest source of [[Protein|protein]] meal in the world. The seed naturally contains mildly toxic erucic acid, while canola is the name for [[Cultivar|cultivars]] with very low levels of it, prized as food for humans and animals. Plants grow to 100 centimeters (39 inches) tall, with bright yellow flowers about 17 millimeters (3⁄4 in) across. Rapeseed is a hybrid of *Brassica oleracea* and *Brassica rapa*. It was cultivated in India as early as 4000 B.C.E. and spread to China and Japan about 2000 years ago. In Europe and Asia it is usually grown in its winter form, sown in autumn. Its oil is also used for biodiesel and industrial lubricants.

Italian painter and architect of the High Renaissance, known in English as Raphael (from Raffaello Sanzio da Urbino). His work is admired for clarity of form, ease of composition and the Neoplatonic ideal of human grandeur. With [[Leonardo da Vinci]] and [[Michelangelo]], he forms the traditional trinity of great masters of the period. He probably trained with Pietro Perugino and moved to [[Rome]] in 1508 at the invitation of [[Pope Julius II]] to work on the Apostolic Palace. There he decorated the Vatican's Raphael Rooms, the central and largest work of his career, which include *The School of Athens*. He also worked as an architect. His workshop executed much of his later work from his drawings. Johann Joachim Winckelmann's influence made his work a formative model for Neoclassical painting, although the [[Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood]] rejected his techniques.

High-capacity [[Public transport|public transport]], usually an electric railway built in urban areas and often called metro or subway. Rapid transit operates on an exclusive right-of-way that pedestrians and other vehicles cannot enter, unlike [[Bus|buses]] or [[Tram|trams]]. Underground lines are called subways, tubes or undergrounds, while elevated lines are called el or skytrains. Trains typically run on railway tracks, though some systems use rubber tires, [[Maglev|maglev]] or [[Monorail|monorail]]. Many systems are increasingly automated, with driverless trains. Initial costs are often very high and mostly government funded, but a well-designed system can bring economic benefits, and transit-oriented development may occur near stations. The world's first rapid transit system, the partly underground Metropolitan Railway, opened in 1863 using [[Steam locomotive|steam locomotives]] and now forms part of the [[London Underground]].

Section of a river with a steep gradient, increased [[Velocity|velocity]] and [[Turbulence|turbulence]]. Rapids lie between a run, a smoothly flowing stretch of stream, and a cascade. The river bed becomes shallower, with some [[Rock (geology)|rocks]] exposed, and splashing water mixes in air bubbles, producing whitewater. Rapids form where the bed material resists [[Erosion|erosion]] better than the bed downstream, so softer rock wears away and leaves an uneven streambed. Four factors are needed: flow, gradient, constriction and obstacles. Constriction narrows channels and speeds the water, while obstacles may come from human activity, landslides, earthquakes or sediment. Rapids aerate the water, improving its quality. They are rated from Class I to Class VI, and the most dangerous class, which poses a threat to life, is often classified as "U" for Unraftable.

One-handed thrusting [[Sword|sword]] with a straight, slender, sharply pointed two-edged blade. It originated in Spain, as the *espada ropera* ("dress sword"), and in Italy. It became popular across [[Western Europe]] in the 16th and 17th centuries as a symbol of [[Nobility|nobility]] or gentleman status, and it was used for [[Duel|dueling]], self-defense and as a military side arm. A typical example would weigh 1 kilogram (2.2 lb) and have a blade 104 cm (41 in) or more in length. Rapier fencing traditions in Spain, Italy and France led to the 18th-century French small sword. The Society of American Fight Directors recognizes rapier and dagger as one of eight main weapon disciplines of stage combat. The English term comes from the French *rapière*.

Vocal delivery combining [[Rhyme|rhyme]], rhythmic speech and street vernacular, usually performed over a beat. Rap is a primary ingredient of [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]] music. It differs from spoken-word poetry in being performed off-time with musical accompaniment, and from [[Singing|singing]] in not relying on pitch. Its components are content, flow and delivery. Precursors include the West African griot tradition, vocal styles of blues and jazz, the African American insult game called playing the dozens, and 1960s African American poetry. Rap music originated in [[The Bronx|the Bronx]], [[New York City]], in the early 1970s, developing from announcements made over the microphone at parties by DJs and MCs. Rap has addressed issues such as [[Racism|racism]] and [[Poverty|poverty]] and political oppression, and by the 21st century it had become a global phenomenon.

American actress and model who became an international [[Sex symbol|sex symbol]] in the 1960s. After *Fantastic Voyage* (1966), she was lent by 20th Century Fox to Hammer Film Productions for *One Million Years B.C.* (1966), in which she had only three lines of dialogue. Posters of her in a doe-skin bikini became bestsellers. She later starred in *Bandolero!* (1968), *Myra Breckinridge* (1970) and *The Three Musketeers* (1973), winning a Golden Globe Award for Best Motion Picture Actress in a Musical or Comedy. In 1995 *Empire* magazine named her one of the "100 Sexiest Stars in Film History."

Any of seventeen lustrous, silvery-white metals: the fifteen [[Lanthanide|lanthanides]], plus [[Scandium]] and [[Yttrium]]. Although not scarce in the Earth's crust, rare-earth elements occur only in compounds, are widely dispersed and are difficult to isolate, so usable ore must be processed in large amounts. They are used in magnets, [[Laser|lasers]], glass, electronics and [[Wind turbine|wind turbines]]. China supplied around 90% of global demand in 2019. The first rare-earth mineral, gadolinite, was discovered in 1787 in a mine at Ytterby, [[Sweden]], which gave four of the elements their names.

French rabbi and commentator, known by the acronym of Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki. Born in Troyes, in northern France, he studied in Worms and later served as head of the beth din in Troyes. He is generally considered the leading biblical exegete of the [[Middle Ages]], admired for presenting the basic meaning of the text concisely and clearly. His commentary on the [[Talmud]], which covers nearly all of the Babylonian Talmud, has appeared in every printed edition since Daniel Bomberg first printed it in the 1520s. His commentary on the Chumash, the Five Books of Moses, is the basis for more than 300 supercommentaries analyzing his choice of language and citations. His surname, Yitzhaki, derives from his father's name, Yitzhak.

First Islamic [[Caliphate|caliphate]], led by the four successive caliphs [[Abu Bakr]], [[Umar]], [[Uthman]] and [[Ali]], known as the Rightly Guided. It led the Muslim community from the death of [[Muhammad]] in 632 to the establishment of the [[Umayyad Caliphate]] in 661. Sunni Islam regards its era as a golden age, although Shi'as reject the first three caliphs. Under Umar, the caliphate conquered more than two-thirds of the Byzantine Empire and nearly all of the Sasanian Empire. Ali's accession triggered the First Fitna, a civil war, and after his assassination in 661 Mu'awiya founded the Umayyad Caliphate.

Indian right-wing Hindutva volunteer paramilitary organization, founded in 1925 in [[Nagpur]]. It leads the Sangh Parivar, a family of Hindutva organizations that includes the [[Bharatiya Janata Party|Bharatiya Janata Party]] (BJP), the ruling party under [[Narendra Modi]]. The RSS is described as having collaborated with the [[British Raj]] and played no role in the [[Indian independence movement]]. It was banned in 1948 after a member, Nathuram Godse, assassinated [[Mahatma Gandhi]], and was later banned during the Emergency (1975–1977) and after the demolition of Babri Masjid in 1992. Critics accuse it of intolerance toward [[Muslims]]. Supporters cite its humanitarian work and non-violent ethos.

Series of low-cost single-board computers originally developed in the [[United Kingdom]] by the Raspberry Pi Foundation with [[Broadcom]]. Created to teach [[Computer science|computer science]] in schools, the Raspberry Pi is also used for industrial automation, [[Robotics|robotics]], home automation, IoT devices and hobby projects. Models offer [[HDMI]] output, [[USB]] ports, wireless networking, GPIO pins and up to 16 GB of RAM, with storage typically on [[SD card|microSD cards]]. In 2015 it surpassed the ZX Spectrum as the best-selling British computer of all time. As of March 2026, more than 75 million units had been sold.
